chapter: Cliff Jackson, Jelly Roll Morton and Harlem in the 1920s
title: Jelly Roll's death, his relatives and the question of his birthplace
summary: After a settlement with RCA Jelly left for California; friends searched for relatives and Caldwell debates whether he was born in New Orleans or Birmingham.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: What happened was that he had -- I think he had a suit against RCA people or either Victor Records, but I think the RCA people were controlling it, and it was somehow or other they'd made a settlement. I think after he got that settlement, that's when he left New York (unintelligible). I was in Atlantic City working with the band. When he left New York driving to California, his first wife was there. She had this hotel. So after he passed, we all, a bunch of us, when we made

the last recording, received letters wanting to know could did we (unintelligible) know anything about any of his relatives. And we started searching around (unintelligible) I said, well, anybody should know, it would be (unintelligible) Wellman Brown, Sidney Bechet or Albert Nicholas, and they were in Europe. Bechet and Albert, they was in Paris then.

So Brod Brode was still in New York, a bunch of us, so they came to get us, one thing, said, I know he had some sisters in New Orleans, that when this guy Lomax wrote worked his book, that he had his sister's name in there and the place where Jelly Roll was born. No, sometime he came up, a kind of a conflict, because I used to go to the YMCA on 135th Street, and this fellow was an old time performer. He was very light, very good performing singer. So we got to talking. He said, listen, do you know where Jelly Roll was born. Said, he was born -- he was from Birmingham, Alabama. He said, Jelly Roll came from New Orleans to Birmingham and played in the theater there, which he did. I said, well then, New Orleans is his home. He said no. I said, well, that's what the book said. He said, well, Jelly Roll's from Birmingham. I said, well, I can't dispute you on that. All I know was that Jelly Roll was from New Orleans, and that's what this book says. But this guy said Jelly Roll was from Birmingham.
But I can't believe it. I think he's just -- the
book tells too many good things about him, be from New Orleans --
-- he was born in Birmingham and went to New Orleans.
